speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawreoce-St. George):
subtopic: FIRST AND SECOND READINGS OF DIVORCE BILLS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, why should senate bills have a preference over other private bills? As a matter of fact, this session we proceeded-as usual, I suppose-by unanimous consent of the house to give the debate on the address precedence, and then again by unanimous consent to give precedence to the debate on the budget, with the result that there has been less opportunity for private bills to be dealt with this session than in any of the previous sessions during which I have been in the house. If this course is continued, it will be impossible in subsequent sessions, unless I very much mistake the temper of hon. members, to secure unanimous consent to precedence of public business. Public business will have to take its proper place on the order paper, and private members will at least have Wednesday afternoons and one hour two nights a week in order to present and discuss their private measures. But under present conditions, with the great mass of private legislation held up without any chance, as it seems to me, of securing the approval of the house during the present session-some of it private legislation which is just as important to the country as many of the public bills that have been introduced-I see no reason why we should give to senate bills precedence over any other private legislation.

I wish to protest as strongly as I can against the disgraceful way in which we are dealing with these divorce cases. I heartily agree with the member who has just spoken with regard to the necessity of having these divorce cases transferred to some court where they can be properly dealt with. At the present time, as we all know, they come before this house and are given three readings, and we are getting into the habit of lumping them together and passing batches of ten, twenty and thirty without giving them the slightest consideration. For some years I sat on the private bills committee where the same thing was done. I doubt whether the ordinary member of the private bills committee read one case in fifty of those coming before him. If some uniusual protest came before the house regarding some particular case we were forced to read the evidence in that case. Although we are supposed to have certain safeguards in this house in the passing of legislation, provided for by a distinct reading three times of each bill and also by dis-

eussion in private committees, as a matter of fact, so far as the house is concerned, there is absolutely no investigation into any one of the cases-not one. I feel that we as members here are not justified, in what is supposed to be, as regards such cases, a more or less judicial committee, in continuing in this most perfunctory way to pass these bills without any investigation whatever. I think, Mr. Speaker, that in the very near future I shall insist that a test case be made in connection with one of these divorce bills and that we discuss in this house the merits of the case. I fancy that if we-did so the first thing we should have to do would be to ask the one lady member oif the house to withdraw. I submit that we are placing ourselves in an unfortunate position if, to avoid publicity of this kind, we condone the manner of granting divorce as at present observed. The house resumed from April 10 consideration in committee of Bill No. 62, relating to the submission to parliament of certain regulations and orders in council.-Mr. Stewart (Edmonton).-Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Hon. CHARLES A. STEWART (Minister of the Interior):	I think a word of explanation
would be in order here. When I explained the provisions of the bill to the house I pointed out that a difficulty arose owing to the fact that all the orders in council passed
[Mr. Card in. 1
in accordance with the statutes had been tabled, but by reason of a neglect extending over a considerable number of years they had not been validated by a resolution of the house and all I was asking to do was to have them validated. It has been pointed out to me since the bill has been under consideration that I am actually doing a little more than that; that I am putting those orders in council in a little different position from what they would be in if they had been simply by resolution validated in the house, and I am going to move an amendment which, I am informed by the Justice department, will place them in exactly the same category as if they had each year been validated by resolutions. I beg to move to amend Bill No. 62 by adding the following sentence at the end of section 1:
Nothing in this act shall operate to place the crown in a better position than it would have been had the said orders in council been approved by resolution in the manner provided by the respective acts.

I mentioned this matter the other day to the Minister of the Interior and he was good enough to place before me a copy of the proposed amendment. I was thinking about it as he was mentioning it and it occurs to me that possibly it should go further and say:
Nothing in this act shall operate to place the crown or any -person in a better position.
I think that is what I had in mind in discussing the matter with the minister. Not only the crown but individuals might be affected by giving the orders in council the force and strength of a statute, which is the effect of the bill. I take'it that the minister does not intend to place either the crown or anybody else in a better position than they would be in if the orders in council had been merely approved. There are orders in council which affect the rights of individuals, and if they had no foundation in law this statute would now make them a valid statute of the parliament of Canada so that the defence that might be open to one individual as against another would be ineffective. I do not suppose it is intended to do more than to say that to the extent to which an order in council had validity, it shall now have validity notwithstanding the fact that it was not approved in the manner prescribed by the act under which it was issued. That is the position; but that need not interfere with the matter, because if the officers of the crown so advise, words can be added

Validation of Orders in Council
when the bill is again before the house. The amendment brings at least the subject matter before the house, and it might be dealt with in that way.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Not having a legal training I am not just sure as to amendment my hon. friend suggests to the amendment I have just moved, but I can assure him that neither the department nor I want any person to be in a superior position to the crown-
No.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: -and if it is necessary from a legal standpoint to add the word "person", then I shall be glad to do so.

It would be a very proper place when the Prime Minister is in his seat to direct attention to the fact that these orders in council-and the minister invited me to inspect them-are very numerous. I should think there must be not less than four or five thousand of them altogether. This brought to my attention the fact that many orders in council affecting public rights are from time to time passed and there is no record of them so far as the public is concerned. I suggested to the minister-and this is not a new suggestion because I had occasion to think it necessary some time ago during the brief period that I was acting in the department-that these orders in council should be published in the Canada Gazette at the end of every month. I can conceive of no other way in which the public interest can be served and in which those interested would have an opportunity of observing just what legislation is enacted by the executive; because after all an order in council has all the effect of a statute, its validity depending upon the statute authorizing it and the order in council being the executive act of the crown's advisers in pursuance of the power conferred upon them by statute. Therefore, so far as the public is concerned, they have all the effect, force and power of a statute. The public in many instances can know and learn nothing unless the order in council is printed in the Gazette. Therefore I suggested to the minister the other day that it is very desirable that such a practice should be followed so that every person concerned might have an opportunity of observing just what executive actions were taken by the government from day to day and week to week in connection with various public interests that are affected by order in council.
I know how difficult at times it has been to follow these matters. In the Poison case it will be recalled that the Privy Council set
aside a judgment that was predicated upon an order in council because the conditions with respect to the publication of the order in council had not been observed. Last night I directed the attention of the minister to a case in which a difficulty had arisen by reason of parliament having taken certain action with respect to an order in council. I am not asking the minister to answer at the moment, but I think all orders in council affecting public properties and public rights should be published in the Gazette as soon as possible after they have been passed; I can conceive of nothing more important in the public interest than that this should be done. For instance, the Department of National Defence has a rule that certain orders in council must be published in the Gazette, and the Department of Interior has a similar rule. I am not now referring merely to the formal business, for instance the cancellation of a quarter-section or something of that sort that requires the action of the governor in council; I am referring to those matters that affect largely public interests and public rights. I think the question of how this can be dealt with is worthy of consideration. In our statute we have only such orders in council published from year to year as may be regarded as important, and the Gazette should be the medium through which the public is informed as to every order in council that affects public interests and public rights.

Does my hon. friend mean, first, all orders in council which affect rights of either individuals or public property, and, second, orders in council which are passed in accordance with the provisions of previous legislation?
Yes.

As a humble member of
the house I wish to protest against this procedure. You have the Liberal party to-day proposing to govern by commissions, by ordei's in council, by governor general's warrants. Although in opposition they condemned all these ways and means. We have to-day this honourable house proposing to pass a bill to validate government by order in council in regard to properties in the western provinces of which no one knows the present value. Even if it does relate to the past it governs also the future. The other day we had before us a bill in regard to the Peace River valley. The Department of the Interior, like the Department of Marine and Fisheries, seems to-day to be nothing but a political machine. Just the other day what did they do

Validation of Orders in Council
by order in council? They granted in effect to Mr. Backus, an American millionaire, a subsidy of $700,000 of the taxpayers' money of this country in connection with his power and light and transportation proposition in the Lake of the Woods district. We have a government in this country that is supposed to consist of the Governor General, the Senate, and the House of Commons, but now it is proposed to take away all the powers of this house in regard to such great questions as those affecting the Dominion lands and Dominion forest reserves and Dominion parks, water powers-mines andi minerals and rule by order in council and delegate to this house powers the potential value of which no one can estimate to-day. The value of these properties not even the minister who presides over the department of the Interior can tell. What this government is doing in connection with the Chicago water diversion is done very largely by order in council.
We have private bills on the order paper today relating to the mergers of the banks of this country, and let me say that the people of this country will soon not own our Canadian banks at all, because American stock-jobbing interests are buying up the stock of the chartered banks of this country in New York. If a bank failed to-day you could not proceed against the shareholders for double liability because the banks are falling into the hands of the Americans, and the stockholders are Americans with no property within the juris-piction of Canadian courts. We have public bills on the order paper seeking amendment to the Insurance Act (lapsed policies) and dealing with bank mergers and water powers, all with the object of protecting the people and the resources of the country, and yet we cannot get these measures discussed at all or passed a first reading simply because they are standing in the names of private members. But a minister of the crown can come down to this house and get amendments to acts relating to our Dominion lands and Dominion forest reserves and parks, and mines and minerals of an enormous potential value and rule by order in council. But the closure rule is applied against the private members. If private members want to put up with that sort of thing, well and good; now is the time to protest and get our rights, but so far as I am concerned, I wish to protest against private members not being allowed to proceed with legislation that is in the interest of the working classes of this country, measures dealing, for instance, with the banks, loans and trust companies, insurance companies, and the exportation of water powers from this country.

Under public orders there are three pages of important progressive public bills standing in the name of private members, and the most consideration they can get all session is a first reading, but there is no difficulty at all when the Minister of the Interior seeks to give Mr. Backus a subsidy of $700,000 to protect his light power and timber domain. Sir Adam Beck was opposed to that measure, so was the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission, and many public bodies in Winnipeg are opposed to it, but it has been made a government bill and passed. Even if it was O.K.'d by the Ontario government, they are not protecting the municipalities to-day so far as the hydro electric movement is concerned, because they have sounded in the Gatineau deal the death knell of the hydro. The Gatineau Power Company and the International Power Company contract makes the Ontario Hydro to-day just a filling station for Mr. Graustein and these big American power companies. As a private member, I protest against this way of doing business by order in- council. This is not a free parliament when a private member cannot bring in and have considered a measure that is in the interests of the public and force it to a vote; it is not a free parliament; we are just degenerating into a mock parliament. We [DOT]have rules which are a hundred years old, and so far as the private member of parliament is concerned, he might just as well go back home and stay there because he can accomplish nothing in this house under the antiquated rules we have. If this is responsible government, all I can say is that it is a sorry day for the people of this country.
The report in regard to the St. Lawrence waterway was brought down to the house only a day or two ago, whereas on the other side of the line it was published in nearly every American newspaper nearly three months ago. I read it myself in the New York Times and the Detroit Free Press about a month ago. Why does not the government give us an oportunity to consider, for instance, the bill standing in the name ofi the hon. member for Leeds, to regulate the exportation of electric power, or the bill standing in my name relating to bank mergers or to lapsed insurance policies? The government will not advance these bills, which are all in the interests of the public, at all. I am surprised that the two Labour members from the city of Winnipeg, who are in favour of public ownership and stand for the public, as far as I can see, do not protest against this way of doing business.

The Labour members are just waiting until they get a chance.

Validation of Orders in Council

You have it now. I wish to protest against this way of doing business. In the Quebec legislature and the Ontario legislature a private member can bring in a bill to amend a government statute, and have his bill read a first and second time, and then have it referred to the private bills committee, where it will receive ample and fair consideration, but when a private member brings a bill into this house which is in the interest of the public, he cannot get it considered at all after a first reading-a fine free parliament! I would appeal to the Minister of the Interior to take over the bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Leeds and give it preferred treatment in this house, and I would suggest to the Minister of Finance, if he wants to do anything to improve the banking law of this country and banking conditions in Canada, that he should find out who owns the eight banks now remaining in this country and take over the bank mergers bill and the lapsed insurance policy bill. Formerly we had eighteen banks in Canada, but now we have only eight, and I venture to say that before parliament reassembles next year, those eight banks will have dwindled down to four or five, unless parliament in the meantime does something to prevent further bank mergers without its consent.
The Prime Minister stated the other day that we would be given an opportunity to discuss the St. Lawrence waterway. He made that statement during the discussion on the motion which I had before the house, and I would have pressed that motion to a vote before six o'clock, but I understood from the Prime Minister that the debate would be reopened after the papers had been brought down, and yesterday we were told that the debate would not be reopened and that we would not be given any special day to discuss that question. I am surprised that the Progressive party does not protest against these antiquated rules. We might as well abolish the House of Commons if we are to have government by commission. The St. Lawrence waterway, the Alberta resources and other economic questions have been referred to the supreme court and commissions; but Mr. Backus is not sent to the supreme court when he wants a hand-out of $700,000 in the shape of water-powers, dams and regulation. I protest against this way of doing business. This is not a free parliament. Hon. gentlemen opposite to-day have abandoned all the principles of Liberalism by introducing this bill A bill similar to this could not get through the British parliament, it could not get through 56103-141
the Australian parliament, it could not get through congress; not one of those bodies would delegate its powers to outside authorities or government by commission or government by order in council. Dear knows who is going to be the next American millionaire to file a claim under the Railway Belt Water Act, the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act, the Dominion Lands Act, the Rocky Mountains Park Act, or the Yukon Act, for some rich timber resources, water-powers or mines and get away with the title deeds and to find Canada a happy hunting ground.

Is it the purpose of this
act to ratify certain orders in council?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, these
are all orders in council which have been cancelled, whatever rights may have existed under them; but the act calls for a resolution validating the orders placed upon the table year by year, and this is necessary because of the failure to take that procedure in former years.
You are not granting new powers or new rights?

They are not all cancelled.

May I ask for a
little fuller explanation of the amendment which I think has been moved? Unfortunately we cannot hear very well at this end of the chamber. It reads as follows, I believe:
Nothing in this act shall operate to place the crown in a better position than it would have been had the said orders in council been approved by resolution in the same manner provided by the respective acts.
I confess that I cannot quite understand this. If it means anything at all, it seems to me it may very easily invalidate the purpose in view.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The object
of the original bill was to validate by statute those orders in council, but under the provisions of the act-this was pointed out to me by the leader of the opposition-we were taking greater power than we would otherwise have had by a simple resolution validating the orders as provided for in the act. This is to give us no more power than we would have had had we simply year by year passed the requisite resolution validating the orders then upon the table. That is why I am



Validation of Orders in Council
inserting in the amendment the word "person" after the word "crown", as suggested by my hon. friend. As amended it will read:
Nothing in this act shall operate to place the crown or any person in a better position than it would have been had the said orders in council been approved by resolution in the manner provided by the respective acts.

After the word
"than" the word "either" should be substituted for "it".

The hon. member for
Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has asked a question that I myself asked when the legislation was first introduced. The fact is the law requires that orders in council shall be laid upon the table, and not ratified by statute but by a resolution. The distinction between the two is of course well known to hon. gentlemen. A resolution does not give any greater validity to the act done under the orders in council than merely to indicate that it was before this -house; but a statute gives it life and validity, whether it was within or beyond the -power of the minister. Having regard to that fact, I pointed out to -my hon. friend that I thought it -desirable to make it clear if an}' orders in council-they are very numerous, some five thousand, extending over a number of years- affected rights and were in law beyon-d the power of the governor in council to pass, it should not be taken that this validation, so-called, g-ave life and validity to what would otherwise have been an illegal act, or an abuse-using the word in its pro-per sense-of the power of the governor in council under the various statutes. So the amendment that has been drawn indicates -clearly that this act of this -parliament -does not give the -crown or any person any greater rights than either would have possessed had the orders in council been approved by resolution, as provided by the several statutes under which they were authorized. I think that sufficiently protects the public interest, although I am bound to say to the hon. minister and the hon. member, that the matter is of very grave concern, for it affects so many orders in council. Until I went through them last night I had no idea how many there were. I suggested to the minister that he might prepare a schedule t-o attach to the act, but it is quite clear that this would be impracticable. A preamble, as my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) suggested, might possibly be inserted, but to give a 'history of all the transactions would involve specifying the numbers of the various orders in council, which in itself would be a considerable task. I think the minister is not quite correct in 
saying that only cancellations are affected, for in turning over the various volumes I recall one that made a grant of public lands thp provisions of the Dominion Lands Act, and another that affected matters dealt with in the Forest^ Act.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I failed to remember that -they go back to 1906.

I noticed that a few did. There is, of course, some force in what the hon. gentleman from Northwest Toronto (Mr. Church) said, that there is grave danger of validating what was not contemplated by the original statute; but I think after the discussion we have had the amendment amply protects the interests of any person that may have been affected either directly or indirectly by reason of the enactment -of this legislation. If the law officers of the crown are satisfied with it, -certainly I should be.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: My instruction to the law officers was not to place us in any better position-
Quite so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: -than we should have been in had the resolutions been passed by parliament year by year.
We simply wish to be assured that in this form it will not do more than that. It seems to me that the amendment as read a few moments ago was rather crude. It referred to a person as " it

speechtext: Thank you.

speechtext: What I instructed the officers to d'o was to prepare an amendment that would leave us in exactly the same position as we should have been in had the orders been validated by resolution. That is all. In the original bill we were doing more than that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The amendment now reads:
Nothing in this act shall operate to place the crown or any person in a better position than either would have been in had the said orders in council been approved by resolution in the-manner provided by the respective acts.

Validation of Orders in Council

Very few members know
what we are doing. How does the minister explain the failure of governments from time to time to bring the resolutions before parliament according to the law? It seems to me that we should have before us a copy of every order in council; otherwise we cannot act intelligently.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
My hon.
friend would need to have considerable time at his disposal to go through them all.
I appreciate that.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that there are no actions pending. On one occasion we were approached by a Winnipeg solicitor with respect to an order in council, and upon following the matter up we discovered-this is the information I received from them-that in the opinion of the officials they were doing their full duty in listing the orders in council and giving them to the minister to be tabled. What would then follow, that is to say the resolution to validate, would be prepared by the officers of the house. This does not in any way affect the order in council except that action might be taken as to the validity of the cancellation of any order.

Since the minister has assured us that this proposed legislation applies merely to the cancellation of certain orders in council conferring rights on individuals, it is far less objectionable than I had thought it to be. At the same time, how can we tell what rights are involved? It may very well be that certain individuals or corporations may have rights that should be recognized, and there is nothing here to protect such rights. We are practically signing a blank cheque and after thait it is left to the administration to carry out. It seems to me, even though this is largely a formal matter, that before we pass it we should have some suoh arrangement as is suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), a sort of schedule giving the number of orders passed, limiting in that way the application of the measure. I do not think that is asking too much, even if the matter has to be held over another year. No one will suffer in the meantime. It has been carried on in this way for a long time and no one has challenged the validity. I think the minister would then be on safe ground. Even although this is legislation of a negative character, I confess I do not like it, because every measure of the kind should be definitely agreed to by parliament itself.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I can assure my hon. friend that where any private rights
56103-141i
were involved no officer of the crown nor any minister would undertake to deny a fiat in order to test the matter in court. That would be unthinkable. On the other hand, where we are dealing with thousands of orders in council it is well that the provisions of the statute regarding them be carried out. Why the slip should have occurred as between 1906 and 1917 I do not know. The explanation I received was that dependence had been placed on the officers of the House of Commons. All the other provisions of the statute have been complied with. I want to impress upon my hon. friend that wherever there was even the semblance of a legitimate claim-wherever any party was prejudiced owing to any act on the part of parliament or of the department- I have never yet refused a fiat to test the question in court. I repeat, that is something that is unthinkable. All these orders in council are in my office and I would lay them on the table, but I am sure my hon. friend would not look at a tenth part of them. No attempt is being made to deprive anyone of any right whatever.
Where does the minister get his authority for saying that this act refers to the cancellation of orders in council? I cannot see any reference to cancellation of orders in council.

I should
have been more explicit in that regard. There may be some orders in council that have not expired.
Water rates in connection with Jasper, for instance.

It simply

I do not like the addition of a section by way of exception to the act, especially as it is better draftsmanship to include it in the only clause of the act. I do not care for the omnibus designation "crown or any person", which of course includes the whole world. If it would be of any assistance to the law officers of the crown

I would suggest this amendment. After the word "approved", in the fourteenth line of the bill, add the words:
and as if the same had been approved, byresolution in the manner provided by the said acts respectively.

speechtext: It means the same thing.
It means the same thing, without lugging in the crown and all and sundry.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I quite
admit that it serves the same purpose, but I should prefer to leave it as it stands. I discussed the matter with the law officers and I have given what they suggest.

It does seem to me that the suggestion is a fair one. Where we are asked to validate some four or five thousand orders in council, it is better that the language should be so expressed as to give only the same validity that these orders in council would have had if they had in due course been approved by both houses of parliament in accordance with the acts mentioned in the the draft bill. Therefore I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryckman) is one which should be considered. As it now stands, the bill provides that orders in council or regulations previously made by the governor in council under the authority of certain acts cited are hereby declared to be and to have been valid, notwithstanding any failure to have the same approved by both houses of parliament as required by the said acts respectively. I would suggest that it should read, "-are hereby declared to be and to have been valid to the same extent as if the same had been approved by both houses of parliament as required by said acts respectively", thereby indicating that we are giving no new validity to the orders in council by reason of a confirmatory statute. I think that would cover all we should be asked to grant, and I believe that is in conformity with the suggestion made by the hon. member for East Toronto.	*

I would draw the attention
of the minister to the fact that all the acts mentioned in this bill have to do with that part of Canada which does not as yet enjoy the right to its own natural resources; this bill refers to the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act, the Dominion Lands Act, and so on. I must confess that I do not quite understand the purport of this legislation, but

we are evidently asked to validate certain orders in council which were made under certain acts the passage of which was felt by many of us to have been a usurpation of power by the Dominion government. I confess that I am suspicious of this legislation.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
These are
only orders in council which were passed under such statutes as the Dominion Lands Act. We are not touching the acts at all.
Since we are now on the verge of placing these resources under the control of those who rightfully own them, I think this legislation might be well postponed for a time.

I am not quite so
optimistic as the hon. member for Rosetown with regard to the transfer of these natural resources to the provinces which legitimately own them. It seems to me that this legislation together with something which was passed a few days ago clearly indicates that the government have not in mind at present the transfer of these resources. If they are contemplating doing so, I think legislation of this kind should be left in abeyance. I understand that a provincial conference has been called for after the close of the session to consider this whole question, so why should anything be done with regard to these natural resources in the meantime unless the government have made up their minds that this provincial conference is only a gesture as far as they are concerned? I think we should have something from the Prime Minister with regard to what the government propose to do, and I think he should tell us something of what they are prepared to place before that conference with respect to the transfer of natural resources.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I must correct my friend at once with regard to a provincial conference. There is no intention to have such a conference with respect to the question of natural resources. The government intend to discuss with the government of Manitoba matters affecting the Manitoba resources; we intend to discuss with the government of Alberta matters pertaining to the natural resources of Alberta, and possibly with the government of Saskatchewan matters pertaining to the natural resources of Saskatchewan. It is not to be a conference of the three western provinces with the Dominion, but separate conferences intended to carry a little further the progress which

Toronto Terminals Railway
has been made already towards a final arrangement which will effect the transfer of the resources.
With regard to this legislation, it has nothing whatever to do with the question of the transfer of the natural resources. Certain orders in council were passed under statutes enacted by this parliament, and those orders in council should have been confirmed by a resolution of this house. Through inadvert-ance on the part of departmental officials those resolutions were not brought to the house, and as a consequence individuals who are fond of raising technical objections or finding reasons which may have some force at law in delaying procedure or invalidating the orders altogether, might be tempted to take advantage of the fact that the procedure called for by the acts has not been fully complied with. The government admit that there has been oversight in the matter in not having these orders confirmed as they should have been. The orders go back, I understand, to 1906, and the whole purpose of this amendment is to ask parliament to say that notwithstanding this omission these orders in council shall stand as though they had been regularized in accordance with the original intention of the legislation, and that in virtue of this legislation no person or the crown shall be put in a better position than would have been the case had the regular procedure been followed.

I have a suggestion to make to the Prime Minister. I would suggest that all the words after "declared" in the twelfth line be struck out and that the following be inserted: "To have the same force and effect as if they had been approved by both houses of, parliament as required by said acts respectively."

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is all
right.
I think that gives them the validity they would have had, which is the intention of the house. I submitted this amendment to the Solicitor General, and he quite aproves of it.

And if that is not accepted, I submit that the amendment as proposed will not do. I submit it would be an arguable case whether an order in council which has been cancelled or a regulation which has been repealed would be set up again notwithstanding the amendment. The possibility' of that situation arising is obviated by the language suggested by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.

We should have some explanation of this bill.

This is the bill which
was referred by the house to the special committee on national railways and shipping, and was there examined in detail. Toronto Terminals Railway
The minister might make a very short statement as to the purport of the bill.

The amount in the
original authority of $7,000,000 for the Toronto viaduct scheme has proven insufficient. It has proven insufficient partly because of changes-the usual changes which take place in the development of a scheme over a period of years-and partly because of the construction of additional facilities for the Canadian National Railways within the terminal area. For instance in the original estimate there was no provision for a Canadian National railway engine terminal which it has been found necessary to erect within the area of the terminals, but which is owned by the Canadian National Railways and not by the terminals company. Another difficulty lies in the fact that with respect to certain property purchases and certain property sales there is quite a difference between the original estimates of the engineers and the actual results in the relative value of these properties. That, I think, is broadly the situation. It is, as my hon. friend I think knows, a joint undertaking between the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Candaian National Railways, and the city of Toronto. I may say that negotiations, subsequent to the original legislation, rather reduced the share of the city of Toronto and increased the share of the railway companies, which again somewhat affects the total amount required.

Will this cover the entire
expenditure and complete the work?

Well, from experience
with large engineering works I seldom take the word of an engineer on such a point until the undertaking is definitely completed. I would prefer not to commit myself to a statement that there will be nothing further, but this at least was estimated to cover all the work which is presently planned in connection with the enterprise.

Would the minister
state the nature of the agreement between the Canadian Pacific, the Canadian National and the city of Toronto?

I have the complete
agreement here but I may say briefly that the undertaking was to create union terminals in the city of Toronto in order to bring all railways into the one terminal. The city was greatly interested in having that result brought about as were also the railways. Following lengthy negotiations, indeed following the commencement of a union passenger 
terminal, this arrangement with the Toronto Terminals Company was brought into being by legislation in 1920. Speaking from memory 50 per cent of the stock is owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway and 50 per cent by the Canadian National Railway Company. As I understand it, the city is not a partner in the terminal company itself but with respect to the cost of the terminals work which affects city streets, city sewers, city parks, and a thousand and one things, there was an apportionment of the cost as between the city on the one hand, and the terminals company composed of the two railways on the other. I cannot say offhand what the city's share is but I will give it to my hon. friend later.
I understand the minister to say that the new agreement reduced the city's obligation.

Oh, no. If I did say that it was not my intention to do so. What I intended to convey was this, that when the original scheme was prepared it was merely an estimate as to what the share of the city would be on the one hand and what t'he share of the railways would be on the other. Subsequently, following the original legislation, an agreement was prepared, and when the principles of the legislation were translated into action the city's share, by virtue of that agreement, did not turn out to be as much as was anticipated when the legislation of 1922 was before the house. I think I have the actual figure here. The city's proportion is $441,000, less than was anticipated when the original legislation was passed in 1922.

I suppose it is quite proper to pass legislation of this character with respect to terminals in the city of Toronto, but I would remind the minister that a similar agreement was entered into between the government, the Canadian National Railways and the city of Quebec. T know that the minister is sympathetic toward the city of Quebec and I hope he will receive with favour the remarks I am about to make. I should like him to try and make Sir Henry Thornton understand that Quebec has some rights in the matter of terminals and that those rights should be considered by the national railway management. An enormous sum of money is being expended upon terminals in Toronto but I do not believe that city was ever callpd upon to pay interest on that investment. On the other hand, altogether different treatment, it would seem, is being extended to the city of Quebec. Therefore I would direct the attention of the Min-

Toronto Terminals Railway
ister of Railways to the railway situation in Quebec and the agreement that was entered into between the Canadian National railways and the city of Quebec under which that city, as I said yesterday, sacrificed a property worth $5,000,000, which represents a great deal of interest on money invested in different improvements, in order to get certain railway improvements and improvements to the port of Quebec.

I would expect in a
case of this kind the Minister of Railways would take up the cudgels for Toronto. Let me assure the hon. member for Quebec-Mont-morency that in this case Toronto is paying fully everything that could be expected from that city. As the matter turns out Toronto does not have to pay as much as it was thought in the first place and what I believe a tribunal decided that it should pay. The fact is that the city pays its own share of the shops. It provides business for this railway, of which we are very proud; it increases the receipts of the Canadian Pacific; it betters the country, and all through you will find that the city of Toronto is paying its full share without help from anybody.

My hon. friend was
scarcely fair to me when he said he did not expect me to take up the cudgels for Toronto.

I said that I would
expect him to do so.

I have made precisely
the same explanation to my hon. friends from Quebec as the hon. member for East Toronto has just made. I can understand the feelings of members representing the city of Quebec when one considers the history of past railway agreements with that city. May I, however, respectfully say that that fact has no more to do with the Toronto terminal than the tirade of the hon. member for Toronto Northeast yesterday had to do with the Quebec harbour? I am merely endeavouring to discuss this question on the basis of a railway business matter and not on the basis of whether it is in Toronto or Quebec or anywhere else. If we have regard to the history of the matter, the railways, through their Toronto Terminals Company, have done very well, and having regard to our experience with similar large expenditures I do not think it has taken a very considerable percentage beyond what was first anticipated, if we take into account what has been added in the way of necessary new work to the original basis on which the original estimate was made.

It is costing forty per
cent more than the estimate.

It would not be correct
to say forty per cent more than the estimate for the work then estimated. For instance, the new engine terminals were not planned in the original work in 1913.
That was an arrangement made between the three railways, the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific.

Exactly, and in the legislation of 1922 I am advised-I was not here at that time and I have had to study the history of the matter-the new engine terminals were not taken into account as part of the expenditure under the statute. They have since proved to be absolutely necessary with the growth of business, the extension of motive power and the construction of the terminals themselves. That has necessitated a great deal of the increase of forty per cent in the expenditure.
I am not the hon. member for Toronto Northeast, but I assume the Minister of Railways referred to me. He has given rise in my mind to the difference between the two situations.

I referred to the hon.
member for Toronto Northeast, not to my hon. friend who has just spoken.

I do not think the
hon. member for Toronto Northeast spoke yesterday.
I mean the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church). I am sorry.

Let me point this out- and it is a lesson to be learned. In my opinion it shows what splendid work has been done by the Department of Railways and by the Canadian Pacific Railway in the city of Toronto. This work is a joint work; it is overseen by both the railways. The terminal company is just the agency of the railways and I believe not a dollar of the expenditure is misplaced. There is no danger of any political heeler receiving any of that money. There is no danger of a job being made for anyone. Every account is strictly audited; every cent is accounted for, and it is to the credit to the railways and, of course, to the Minister of Railways, that that situation exists.	.
Toronto Terminals Railway

There is only one point
in this bill to which I wish to refer and that is why the amount is being increased from $7,500,000 to $10,500,000. The city of Toronto has contributed $32,000,000 to rebuild the harbour plus $10,000,000 for the cost of the viaduct making $42,000,000 in all for grade separation and waterfront development. The chairman of the railway board found that the city was not liable for any part of this cost of grade separation, inasmuch as the Railway Act did not provide for it, and the city went in voluntarily. Many years before the agreement known as the Toronto viaduct agreement of 1913 was entered into in regard to the division of the cost between the Canadian Pacific, the Grand Trunk and the city, it was decided that the city was not obligated for one cent. What we say to the committee is this, that Toronto is the only city in the Dominion that is to-day paying for grade separation an amount of about $43,00,000 all told. A large part of the Sunnyside harbour improvements east of the Humber river was for protection of the right of way of the national railways and the city has expended more than $5,000,000 there. As regards the Canadian National in Toronto, a large part of this extra money is to provide for the Canadian National's share of the cost of the new Union station, and works ancillary to the viaduct. I may put the situation in three or four paragraphs in Sir Henry Thornton's own words when he was giving evidence before the select standing committee on railways and shipping. The Minister of Railways said that, to start the ball rolling, he would ask the question:
Why the increase from $7,500,000 to $10,500,000?
Sr Henry Thornton: The amount of money asked for is for certain works which are ancillary to the construction of the Toronto terminal, and which have grown out of the Toronto viaduct proposition. For example, it was necessary to construct for the exclusive use of the Canadian National railways an engine house, and a number of other things of that character have been necessary and have been occasioned by the Toronto viaduct and the new Toronto terminal.
Mr. Jelliff: What was the cost of the rew engine house?
Mr. Brown: The engine house and coach facilities, about $2,000,000.
Sir Henry Thornton: In addition to the engine house there was an additional express house and express facilities; there were jfiices for the Canadian National railways, which represented $300,000. The finst item, "express facilities," amounted to $346,000. There was also a power house, which was not originally included. which represented $665,000. That totals $1,306,000. In the adjustment of our relations with the city, the city was unable to bear as large a proportion of some of the expenses as

we expected, and that had to be cared for. There was also a difference of about $1,000,000 in regard to land. We expected to get about $3,000,000 for certain lands we were going to sell, but we only got $2,000,000. Briefly, this represents necessitous work which had to be done as growing out of the construction of the Toronto terminal.
Mr. Jelliff: Work not contemplated in your original arrangement?
Sir Henry Thornton: Partly not contemplated, and partly underestimated.
Hon. Mr. Stevens: Does this $10,500,000 represent the total investment of the National railways in the Toronto viaduct?
Sir Henry Thornton: No, the total cost of the Toronto viaduct-
Mr. Brown: It will be about $17,500,000.
Hon. Mr. Stevens: The National Railways' participation will be about $17,500,000?
Sir Henry Thornton:	Eventually, yes.
Hon. Mr. Stevens: Including the station?
Sir Henry Thornton: Yes.
Hon. Mr. Stevens: All the terminals?
Sir Henry Thornton: Yes.
Hon. Mr. Stevens: And the viaduct?
Sir Henry Thornton: Yes.
Mr. Milne: Has the C.P.R. a like amount invested as compared with the C.N.R.?
Sir Henry Thornton: I should think approximately. yes.
