speechtext:
The proportion between the two you would say is about half and half?
Sir Henry Thornton: Yes.
Hon. Mr. Stevens: Is the seventeen millons in addition to the ten and a half?
Sir Henry Thornton: No, the seventeen million is the total.
The city of Toronto has contributed $32,000.000 to eliminate all these level crossings, and one-third of the amount of the cost of the viaduct, $10,500,000. This bill is for $7,500,000 for ancillary works for the Canadian National, growing out of the viaduct, namely, a new engine house, express terminals, offices, land and incidentals.

I would not for one moment oppose any vote for Toronto. I think that Toronto is entitled to the greatest possible consideration from this house. I think all the members on this side of the house will agree with me in saying that Toronto is a magnificent city and a magnificent port, one which will no doubt one day become an ocean port, and certainly we should not begrudge one cent to Toronto provided there can be shown some justification for the expenditure. There is no sectional feeling on this side of the house, I can assure my hon. friend of that. I sat silent in my seat yesterday listening to my hon. friends opposite assuring me that they loved Quebec, though, may I add, with a purely platonic friendship, because we do not get much from them. I have the same feeling of affection for Toronto as they have for Quebec.
As I understand this vote, it was originally intended to permit the city of Toronto, in con-

Toronto Terminals Railway
junction with the two railways, to bring the railways into the city, but unfortunately they began apparently by putting the cart before the horse; for they built a magnificent station in the centre of the city of Toronto and then came to parliament to ask us to purchase the necessary property and to build tracks into that station. That may be the proper procedure, but we in Quebec, not having had the benefits of any favours from the Canadian National Railways, are not in a position to say whether it is or not. In any ease the fact is that millions of dollars have been spent on a station in Toronto, and then parliament is asked to bring a railway into that station.
The station was built by the railways.

It is immaterial to me by whom the station was built. The fact is that the station was built, and then parliament is asked to vote millions to bring the railway to it. In our part of the country we build the railway first and then think about the station. That brings me to the point I wish to bring before the committee. As I said before, there is no objection to voting this money for Toronto, even although the estimate has been materially increased and there is no assurance that the revenues are going to be any higher than before.

I am sure they will
not be.

I am quite sure that if
the Minister of Marine and Fisheries had admitted in this house yesterday that there would be no justification for the Quebec harbour vote from an increased revenue standpoint there would have been a howl from all sides of the house, but here is the Minister of Railways boldly, and almost brazenly, telling this house that we are expending offhand $84,000,000 or $35,000,000 for which there is no justification from a revenue standpoint.
Oh, no.

It is the most extraordinary statement I have heard from a minister of the crown in the last ten years.	.
Following the line of the argument which has been developed in this house, and which I think is a most effective and a logical one, we in the city of Quebec have been asking for station terminal accommodation from the Canadian National Railways, and at one
period of our existence, thinking that we might obtain some favour from the government if we gave them something, we handed over to the railway property worth $2,000,000.

My hon. friend was mayor
of the city of Quebec at the time, and he should know. We handed that amount over to the Canadian National Railways on condition that they would give us something in return. But not only did we receive nothing in return, but the Canadian National Railways instead of building a station, rented accommodation from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in Quebec. At the present time the Canadian government railway is paying something like half a million dollars a year to the Canadian Pacific Railway in order that Canadian National trains may run into the city of Quebec, in spite of the fact that a site for the building of the station has already been given to the railway by the cits'- of Quebec itself in order that proper terminal facilities should be built. We naturally think that fhe Canadian National Railways, before seeking such an enormous sum for Toronto, should show some consideration for the smaller communities in this country, and we think that a small community like Quebec, though possibly it does not produce such returns to the Dominion as other larger communities, should at any rate receive reasonable accommodation and get something in the way of a station and terminal facilties of which the country need not be ashamed. I do not wish to stress the point with reference to Montreal, because I see my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George in his seat, and to my knowledge he has never missed an opportunity of setting before parliament and the country the claims of the city which is distinguished by having him as its representative, and when the proper time comes, I am sure that he will see to it that that rat-trap which is called Bonaventure station is torn down and a proper station built in the metropolis of Canada. It would perhaps have been well for his own sake and the sake of his city if he had had a measure of that kind tacked on to the bill which is now before us. He might have had more chance of getting it through-not that I wish to make any insinuation about what is called in the United States logrolling-

We are casting our bread
on the waters now, expecting a return later.
Toronto Terminals Railway

Does my hon. friend expect any gratitude in politics? If so, I am surprised that he should still retain after so long a political experience some of the illusions of his youth. So far as I am concerned I should like him to see to it, whenever he wants anything for Montreal, that it is tacked on to something else, though not to something for Quebec. Of course we have always believed that anything that benefits Montreal benefits Canada, and we have always said so, though perhaps not out loud. Now, Mr. Chairman, I did not desire to take up so much of the time of the committee.

Elaborate further your
love for Toronto.

On a previous occasion when this matter was discussed I said it was a good thing that Toronto should be beautified, at least on the exterior, that it would be of advantage to the Dominion for strangers to find Toronto a beautiful city. If they do not remain there very long, so much the better for the reputation of the city. I hope the minister and the members for Toronto will take my observations in good part-especially the latter, for whom I have such an undying love. I hope that on some other occasion they will not forget the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, but live in hopes that some day one good turn will deserve another. If I do not strenuously oppose this measure, but simply call the attention of the minister to the fact that other communities throughout the Dominion are really in need of government assistance, and ask him to cast his benign glance on the district from which I come, then I think I shall hare done my duty to my country and to the constituency which I represent.

I think the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) overlooked the fact that we have a Canadian National Railway terminal station in Quebec city. It was erected on the very valuable property known as the Champlain market site on the harbour frontage, which was handed over to the railway by the city of Quebec. This station was built two years ago at the enormous cost of 825,000! In 1910 under the agreement then entered into between the Canadian Natioanal Railways, the government and the city of Quebec, it was arranged to build a station at a cost of two million dollars. Tenders were called, and contracts were let. Then in 1911 came a change of government, and all those plans, which had been prepared by railway, steamship and other experts, were
[Mr. Cahan.J
set aside, and this little 825,000 station was substituted for the two million dollar structure. To-day the Canadian National Railways system brings passengers into Quebec and hands them over to the Canadian Pacific Railway hotel. Year after year we have been asking for the terminal facilities that were promised us, but without success. I think that Sir Henry Thornton, who seems to have so much time to spare, should give more attention to the rightful demands of the city of Quebec and remedy the very unsatisfactory situation which we now have to endure.

Might I say, Mr. Chairman, that this is a triplicate agreement to build the Toronto viaduct at a cost of thirty-three million dollars, of which the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Canadian National Railways and the city each bear a third. All the works ancillary to the viaduct are to be paid for by each of the parties. Recently Sir Henry Thornton told a committee of this house that the central regional area of the Canadian National Railways yields about 75 per cent of the whole revenue of the system. The Laurier administration took 8122,000,000 credit and 823,000,000 cash out of the old Grand Trunk in the central region and put it into Quebec to build the Grand Trunk Pacific.

I do not want to encourage any sectional discussion as to where the revenues of the Canadian National Railways come from and where they are expended. I do not think either the management or parliament would desire the system to be run on that basis, but rather on the basis of rendering the best possible sendee to the country as a whole. With regard to my statement which the hon. member for Quebec South described as "bold and brazen", it does happen to be the truth. Whether or not the condition is similar to the condition in respect of Quebec harbour, which was dealt with yesterday by my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, is neither here nor there. But it is a fact with respect to our large terminals, more especially Toronto and Montreal

there are others-that our two railway systems are facing in the not distant future tremendous expenditures on improved facilities, expenditures which cannot in the nature of things increase the revenues of the railways at all proportionately. Reference was made by the member for Quebec South to what he described as the "rat-trap" Bona-vent-ure station at Montreal. I say quite frankly that I do not know of any city of the size of Montreal with railway terminal conditions at all comparable with those now ex-

Toronto Terminals Railway
isting there so far as the Canadian National is concerned. The Canadian Pacific conditions in Montreal are of course considerably better; bub it is well known that the Canadian National conditions are very bad indeed. Due to the merging of the former government line, the former Canadian Northern Line and the former Grand Trunk Line, we have a very difficult situation indeed in Montreal which will cost a great deal of money to bake care of, involving an investment which, I repeat, cannot produce an increased revenue in proportion. Such investments do however tend to reduce expenditure in operating along some lines, but even in that connection it is too much for this parliament to hope that the large expenditure which will be necessary in these congested terminals will represent a revenue at all proportionate to the outlay. Even a considerable contributory factor cannot be looked for. The expenditures must be made, both from the point of view of public safety and of giving service to the public. The entrance to the city of Montreal over the Canadian National lines at the present time, as is well known, with its number of level crossings, gates and so forth, is a constant source of danger. That condition has to be faced on every railway system wherever there is a quickly growing centre of considerable size. In Toronto we have got along very far with the work. And it has been expensive work. It will not tend to increase the revenues of the railway; in some measure it may tend to reduce expenses of operation, although not in any very great measure even in that direction. We have the Montreal problem to face, and the Quebec problem is of a slightly different character, -as the city is not of such great size, and the terminal is not so congested. But there again we have another problem. In the cities of Ontario and in the west, to a greater or lesser degree, we have this terminal problem to deal with, and during :he next ten or fifteen years at the outside it will be necessary for the railways of Canada, not only the Canadian National, to face the question of relatively unremunerative expenditures on improved terminal facilities.

I have no desire to prolong
the discussion, but there is one point which it might be advisable to make clear. It seems to me there is a misapprehension, either imaginary or real, on the part of my hon. friend from Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lavigueur) regarding this bill. One would imagine from what he has said that the city of Toronto was receiving in this connection a grant or gift or loan, with or without interest, or something of that sort. He shakes his head; if I am wrong I shall be glad to withdraw the suggestion. But when he discusses this question in connection with Quebec and evinces what seems to be a desire to get back a little bit at some of the discussion that took place yesterday and the day before, it does give me the impression that he is under a misapprehension. The city of Toronto as a municipality is getting nothing whatever out of this legislation in any shape or form. This is nothing more than an authorization from parliament to enable the Canadian National Railways to issue bonds for the sum of money in question in order that they themselves may carry on their undertaking in that city. Whether the stand some of us took regarding Quebec was right or wrong, this matter certainly is not in any shape or form a parallel with the Quebec harbour resolution. The whole of the Canadian National Railways will become responsible for the repayment of these bonds when they are issued.

Mr. Chairman, when I shall next meet my constituents, they will certainly ask me to explain the vote that I shall cast to-day. We are asked to vote 810,500,000 to the Canadian National for improvements to the station at Toronto. Each time that the least thing is asked for my county, even if its is simply a spot where our farmers can sit down and relieve themselves of their parcels while awaiting the train, we are told: if you can guarantee us some return we shall accede to your request. Will there really be, in the present case, an increase in earnings which, even in the first year, will pay the interest and a portion of the sinking fund on the amount we are asked to vote? You are aware, Sir, that such will not be the case. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) told us a few moments ago that this could not be.
Wlien the house was discussing, yesterday, a loan to the Quebec Harbour Commission, we were told: Gentlemen, you have not paid any interest, nor have you a sinking fund for your prior loans. These gentlemen, Sir, sitting on your left were shocked and asked for a special committee to investigate the matter. Why do they not ask for a special committee, to-day, to inquire if really the amount asked for will bear interst the very first year.
May I ask the hon. Minister of Railways if he can point out, in the Province of Quebec, one single railway station which is in keeping with the earnings to which we con-
Toronto Terminals Railway

Mr. Chairman, I read
in the Ottawa Journal yesterday that the Quebec members had been dumb this year. After all we have heard in English from hon. gentlemen across the way about the love they have for Quebec, I think this is a good opportunity to reciprocate in French, and tell the committee about the love of Quebec for Toronto.
(Translation):	Mr. Chairman, this is certainly a special opportunity for us, members of the rural districts, to discuss the question of railway stations. I wish to assure the house that our feelings, like those of the hon. members for Ontario who spoke yesterday, are of the best.
We do not wish to criticize the amount which it is proposed to grant Toronto for the

Toronto Terminals Railway
embellishment of its station, however there is one thing which must be borne in mind: there alsix exists beside large towns, small centres which deserve consideration. In our Chicoutimi and Lake St John districts, located on the other side of the Laurentian hills, the only means of communication we have is the national railway. Some years ago, the city of Quebec and the provincial government made quite a considerable grant to the Lake St. John railway to further its expansion and give us suitable stations. Now what strikes us on our arrival at Quebec, at the station known as that of Parent square? There is not a shed, there is not a station site throughout the whole system of the national railway, from ocean to ocean, which can compare in ugliness and discomforts with this station The same may be said on our arrival in Montreal, at the station known as the Moreau station. The Bonaventure station is a palace compared with the Moreau street station, where there is not even a suitable waiting room, and where in winter the wind not only penetrates through the windows but also through the walls, to the great discomfort of the travelling public. We should be treated in a more decent manner, because of all the lines of the Canadian National, there is not one which equals the Chicoutimi, Lake St. John, Montreal and Quebec line, in volume of both passenger and freight traffic. The mills erected within the last few years ship by the means of this railway thousands and thousands of tons of freight, and the travelling public which congregate there from all parts of Canada, when getting off at a station, find only sheds. And as just stated by the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Dussault), when we ask for improvements, we are answered: the traffic and returns do not justify such a step. The amount which it is proposed to grant for the Toronto station, even the half of it would allow us to have suitable stations from one end to the other of the railway in the districts which I have just mentioned. It is more than time to grant us the improvements which have been asked for ever so long. It is not only a question of comfort but also one of public safety and hygiene. It is most discouraging to observe the condition of stations especially between Quebec and Chicoutimi. The length of trains has increased considerably, within the last few years, with the result that platforms have become too short; people are forced to alight from trains at some distance from the platform, in the mud or dirt. Accidents have even happened owing to this state of things. The same condition exists as regards the cars themselves. I acknowledge and I am aware that the railway company has certainly made considerable improvements, however in view of the expenditure which we are making for other localities, for the embellishment of large towns and especially for that of Toronto, we are entitled to request not things of a decorative (nature, but decent improvements. I therefore take the opportunity to repeat my request to the hon. Minister of Railways, so that he may insist, with his advisers as well as with the President of the National Railways, that urgent improvements be carried out from one end to the other of our line. I am not criticizing what is being done elsewhere but I am simply asking that a small portion of the enormous sums spent elsewhere be granted to us.

When this estimate was before the committee on railways and shipping I took the trouble to direct the attention of the chairman of the national system and his officials to the condition that existed on the railway in the lower part of the province of Quebec, the condition of our railway platforms and of our stations; and I even went as far as to say that that part of the eastern division was, as we say down there, the "orphan' section. I took occasion also to direlct the attention of the officials of the Canadian National Railway to the quite apparent discrimination that existed as between the treatment accorded to the eastern division on the one hand and to the remainder of the system on. the other. Personally I have no objection whatever to the proposed expenditure for Toronto; but, sir, it seems to me that in justice to our own section of the country it would be advisable for the minister, if he could do so, to vouchsafe us an inkling as to what is going to be done to remodel the station at Quebec, to say nothing of stations elsewhere. I understand there is an agreement between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National as to the use of what is called the central station at Quebec. I also understand that a tentative program has been prepared by the officials of the national railway to provide adequate station accommodation. I should like to know if the management of the system intend to submit this program to the committee on railways and shipping at its next meeting, or later on when the estimates for the system are being considered. In the second place I shoulld like to know if it is the intention of the management to treat the eastern section as really a part of the system. We are afraid that owing to the deficit on the eastern section being made good by parliament, the management are disinclined to undertake any expenditures whatever in connection with that section. I do hope that these matters will be brought
Toronto Terminals Railway

to the attention of the manager of the system and that by inaugurating improvements he will make it manifest thait we are entitled to consideration notwithstanding the fact that parliament has to make good any deficit on the eastern division.

Plans for station accommodation in Quebec have been under the consideration of the management for some time past. As to whether definite conclusions have been reached, I cannot say from memory. I can, however, say that my hon. friend and the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) are both members of the committee on national railways and shipping, and therefore can obtain any information from the officials before that committee with respect to station plans anywhere. I know my hon. friend will take advantage of his opportunity in that regard.
As to the general question of the eastern line, I may say that I have not found the management backward at all in making the necessary expenditures in that region since the Maritime Rates Act came into force. As a matter of fact I rather fear consequences opposite to those feared by my hon. friend. Very naturally when those managing a railway are aware of the fact that any deficit in operation will be borne from the national treasury instead of charged against the system they are not likely to be more miserly, shall I say, than they would be if deficits were charged to the system treasury instead of being voted by parliament as the Maritime Rates Act contemplates. I think my hon. friend is very capable of looking after the necessities of his own section, especially as now, in consequence of an act which passed this house a few days ago, he will have an opportunity, in regard to matters of maintenance and otherwise, to go to the railway commission and get an order from that body the same as is possible in the case of railways in other parts of the country.
I did not catch the remarks of the hon member for Lake St. John (Mr. Sylvestre) in their entirety, owing to my non-familiarity with the Frendh language, but I gathered that he is calling attention to the lack of decent station accommodation in the province of Quebec.
Especially in the province of Quebec.

As regards Canada generally there are very few cities where first class terminal railway accommodation exists. The terminal facilities at Toronto are not yet completed, and speaking offhand I cannot think of any city, outside of Winnipeg, on the

Canadian National, where it may be said that the terminal conditions are reasonably adequate. At Winnipeg, owing tj, the tremendous volume of grain needing to be handled, action with respect to terminal facilities was expedited. I think it may be said from the point of view of adequacy that the Winnipeg terminals, which were undertaken before the Canadian National came into being, are possibly the most up to date; but otherwise-and it is true not only of the province of Quebec but of every other province in the Dominion-we have not yet established what would be regarded in other countries as the type of terminal facilities required for great cities; we have been too busy stretching out in order to serve the country generally. Nor have we yet done very much in the way of providing what may be described as the frills of a railroad. Indeed it may be some years yet before we are able to meet that condition satisfactorily.

The minister stated a few minutes ago that the provision of terminals in other cities, especially in Montreal and Quebec, would have to be considered in the near future. He also stated that an enormous amount of money had been spent in the city of Toronto and that the work is not yet completed. He might have said that this expenditure runs into hundreds of millions when the waterfront of Toronto is taken into account.
We have built a new city hall too, don't forget that.
If I may be permitted I would suggest that this matter be allowed to stand until it has been investigated by a special committee.

The hon. member has
spoken of the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars in Toronto when the cost of the viaduct will only be $33,000,000.
But I was referring also to the enormous sums expended on the waterfront at Toronto which, of course, came from the national treasury.
The hon. gentleman is having recourse to poetic licence.

I do not think there is any reason for urgency in this matter. It can well stand over until it has been investigated. There should not be any greater hurry to vote this amount of money than there was when we were asked to vote money for the Quebec harbour, in connection with which the suggestion was made that the matter be investigated by a committee of the house.

Toronto Terminals Railway

This matter has been
investigated by a committee.

Yes, but I should like to see more than that. I should like to see the matter investigated by a special committee which should be given power to inquire into the question of terminals in Montreal, Quebec and other large cities as well as Toronto. My fear is that after the $33,000,000 have been granted and spent in Toronto, when we come to ask for reasonable terminal improvements in other cities, parliament and the railway authorities may say to us: We have spent so much money in Toronto that we shall have to let this matter stand for some time. The result will be that the city of Quebec, which has been waiting so long to get justice, will, as usual, again have to wait for the good will of parliament and of the railway authorities in the matter of getting some kind of decent railway facilities. I suggest to the minister and the committee that this matter should stand and that a special committee be appointed to consider the advisability of granting a reasonable amount of money for railway terminals in the other large cities I have mentioned as well as in Toronto.

Mr. Chairman, I have but a few words to add as I do not wish to delay any further the committee. As the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Sylvestre), mentioned a short while ago, in answer to the Ottawa Journal which intimated that less French speeches are heard this year than in previous sessions, I wish to state that if we do not make use oftener of our mother tongue, it is because the majority of members in the House cannot follow us.
I wish to support the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset), who a short while ago told us of the difficulties encountered in the eastern portion of our province in obtaining necessary improvements in the way of fences and ditches. Personally, since I have the honour of representing the riding of Montmagny, I have had great difficulty in obtaining work of that nature. I must congratulate the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), for having so smoothed the way as to enable us now to apply to the Railway Commission in order to obtain these improvements, instead of applying to the board of management of railways, as it has been the practice heretofore, without the slightest chance of success. The present bill under discussion requests that we should vote
810,500,000	to build a station at Toronto. Quite so, but if the city of Toronto wishes this embellishment, I think that its contribution should be greater. After all, this is in the interest of the city of Toronto; the object, if I am not mistaken, is to lessen accidents and so forth. If the government is to help in the embellishment of Toronto, I think that this city should itself contribute more effectively.
While we are on the subject of stations,
I wish to tell the committee that there are still in my riding two stations which are not provided with electric lights. It strikes me that in the year 1928, there should not exist any stations lighted by lamps; it is certainly not very satisfactory for the travelling public. This goes to show that we are entirely deprived of modern improvements which, after all, are not more costly than the old methods of lighting. It cannot be gainsaid that this part of the national railway, which in the past was known by the name of Intercolonial, is the most paying portion of our railways. For the last few years it is with the profits realized on this portion of the national railways that the board of directors has been able to meet the deficits of the other parts of the system. It seems to me that if the traffic is sufficiently large to realize such considerable profits, this section of the national system should be treated as fairly as other parts of the Dominion. If the sections of the national railways to the east of Sainte-Rosalie, Levis and Quebec are the most paying ones, we certainly have a right to request equal treatment with the other parts of the national system. It is our duty while discussing this bill, to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways to the existing conditions in this part of the province of Quebec, in order that he may advise the management of the national railways to grant us what we request simply because it is fair to do so.

Mr. Chairman, since it is a question of an expenditure of $10,500,000, and the earnings which may be derived from such an investment, would it not be possible to obtain from the hon. Minister of Railways, a statement of returns and expenditure for the various sections of the Canadian National Railways. We maintain that the two sections from Montreal to Levis, and Levis to Campbellton, are the best paying sections of the national railway system, but we have never been able to obtain from the management of the national railways the statements which would allow us to establish before this house the financial situation as it exists in regard to net profits in the various sections. This is very detrimental to us.
To-morrow the western members will ask this house to vote them money for branch
Toronto Terminals Railway

lines, when the main line in their districts does not even pay any interest on the outlay of its construction. The main line in certain localities return but deficits, yet we are asked to vote $2,000,000, $3,000,000 and $4,000,000 to further build branch lines, and we comply. We vote those amounts because we do not really know what are the various sections in this country that are responsible for the surpluses or deficits of our railways. We are asked $10,500,000 for improvements in the city of Toronto. Does the management of the various railway sections around Toronto show surpluses or deficits? We are anxious to know. We are asked to vote this amount, while on the other hand we are told by the Minister of Railways that this expenditure of $10,500,000 will produce no further earnings and will only be for the embellishment of the city. Must we vote such amounts for the embellishment of the city of Toronto?
If the city of Montreal has been able to earn such good returns heretofore with the only station of Bonaventure, I wonder why Toronto cannot wait ten years more with the present station which is a much better one than that of the national railways at Montreal. Unless we get further explanations. I do not think that the house can vote this amount.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN CREDIT INSTITUTE
speechtext:
The bill was thoroughly
discussed in the private bills committee, and it passed that committee without any controversy save for one or two very slight amendments. The purpose of the bill is set forth in clause 2:
The objects and powers of the institute shall be:

(1) To organize, promote, operate and control a national institute of credit men and to examine into and improve conditions relating to the work of credit men throughout Canada.
Then it goes on to specify the manner in which those objects shall be accomplished.
The idea behind the bill briefly is this, that it is desirable now to have uniformity in the standards, and to improve the standards, of credit men who are engaged by commercial houses throughout Canada. Formerly, every man who was engaged in business knew his customers personally, and knew the extent of credit that he might safely afford to them, but that time is now past. Our business houses to-day are engaged in business the ramifications of which extend from one end of Canada to the other, and it is impossible for the proprietors of them to know personally their customers and the amount of credit that may safely be extended to them. In addition, much of the business of Canada is now being conducted by corporations, and the business of many of these corporations is not confined to a particular part of the country but extends throughout the various provinces. In order that a man may be assured that the credit department of his business is being properly run, it is desirable to have some sort of institute at which credit men can be properly trained, and being so trained can get from the institute a certificate that they are thoroughly familiar with credit matters. The purpose, therefore, is to set up a Canadian institute of credit men which shall have power to set examinations and grant certificates to the members who have qualified. The business men of this country who are seeking a competent credit man can then have some degree of assurance that they are getting a qualified man from the fact that he has become a member of the Canadian credit institute.
The jurisdiction of this parliament to incorporate an institute of this sort is, I think, entirely beyond dispute. There will be nothing to prevent provincial legislatures from incorporating provincial credit institutes. The Dominion of Canada has already incorporated similar associations-the Dominion association of chartered accountants, for instance, which was organized in 1902 along similar lines to those proposed here. Similar legislation was passed in 1913 with regard to general accountants, and later with regard to stationary engineers, and so on. I think that answers the question of my hon. friend.

He ought to be here as the leader of parliament to note the difficulty in which the house now finds itself, and the very great danger of making sport out of perhaps some of the most serious breaches that are brought to the attention of parliament. We have undoubtedly during the last half hour been making parliament more or less of a farce in the case of seventy-five bills that I hold in my hand and anyone of which might very well be and is undoubtedly a serious human tragedy. Let me say this in answer to the request made by the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) for certain details. I might preface that word with the word "sordid" and say "sordid details". I am sure that neither I nor any other hon. member desires to have these details read to the house. In fact, if he will glance at the language in the preamble to this bill, he will find there a complete answer to his query, an answer that I am quite sure no one desires to read nor to treat frivolously; but there it is.
This brings me to the question of our method of procedure in dealing with this bill as with other similar bills. These unfortunate people, in one respect blameworthy people, bring their suit in the senate and before a committee of the senate their case is tried. There is no committee of parliament that is held in higher regard throughout the Dominion of Canada than the committee of the senate which sits on divorce.
And no court.

I was coming to that.
There is no committee of parliament that discharges its duty more faithfully and with more judicial care, thought and procedure than the committee of the senate on divorce. Furthermore, I had occasion this week to

discuss the matter with two very able lawyers, friends of mine, not members of the house, and I question whether there is a divorce court in provinces where such courts exist, or any other court in Canada that treats the subject matter brought before it more carefully and judicially than does the divorce committee of the senate. Therefore I submit to my hon. friends that this case, the immediate bill before us, being Bill No. 74, letter E of the senate, having gone to that court, having been dealt with, the evidence having been heard in all its sordid details and the bill having been passed on to us, it is unnecessary for the house or for the private bills committee to go into extreme details in the matter unless the decision of the senate committee is called in question. In such a case the House of Commons acts in a measure as a sort of court of appeal, but in none of these cases has the bill been called in question. In every instance, so far as I know, both sides have concurred in or at least have not complained of the decision. I suggest that we should cease the controversy. On the one hand I appeal to the government as the leaders of the house-if the Prime Minister were in his seat I would appeal to him frankly to face the situation that has arisen and that will arise again next year-I have forgotten the number but I think there are two hundred and some odd divorce bills before parliament this year-and to allow parliament to disentangle itself from the mess in which it finds itself involved. On the other hand I appeal to my hon. friends to my left to allow these bills to pass in the usual orderly manner so that we may proceed with the business of parliament and not make a farce out of wihat is a most serious human tragedy.

I rise largely to concur in the main with what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre has just said. I desire however to point out that even if the senate bill, which now stands as a public bill, were dealt with and passed by the house, the problem of the 'house dealing with divorce bills would not be entirely eliminated. Under our rules it would still be possible for any hon. gentleman to do what hon. members have been doing to-night, because divorce would still be granted with respect to the people of some provinces, one province at any rate, in the manner which has been prevalent in Canada since confederation. We would merely to some extent lessen the difficulty; we would not altogether remove it.

I agree that we would remove it to a large extent. I would point out however that it is and has always been possible for obstruction of the kind we have experienced to-night to take place, and I am finding no fault with hon. gentlemen. I know their motive is to force this question. What they desire to do is to substitute another court for the court of parliament in connection with this matter. But I submit that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was entirely right in his description of the dignified and proper manner in which these cases have been tried. It is not correct to allow the impression to go out to the country that parliament does not give proper and judicial consideration to these divorce bills. It is true that it has not been the custom of this chamber to give such consideration. The court has been set up in the senate for many years and the judicial committee of the senate which tries these cases supplies us with the evidence. When the bills come before this chamber it is competent for every hon. member to read the evidence in connection with every case and to make a specific objection on a specific bill if in his judgment the evidence there recorded does not warrant the action of parliament in the matter. Therefore while we may have objections to this method of granting divorces, we should not convey to the country by our actions or by our speeches the impression that divorce is lightly granted by the parliament of Canada. In reality divorce is less lightly granted by parliament than by any court in Canada or indeed by any court that I know of anywhere else. Whatever objection we may have to the procedure, there is possible through the machinery of parliament, a more complete check upon divorce than exists in the machinery of the courts. I do not think the lawyers in the house will disagree with that statement. I join with my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre in appealing to the committee to maintain the dignity of this House of Commons and to proceed in the regular manner with these bills, having regard to the evidence which is printed and in our hands with respect to every particular case.

Just before nine o'clock may I remark that if I made what appears to have been a formal and technical objection, I did so in order to add weight to the words of the hon. member for Wetaskiwan who said that when a person introduces a bill of this kind, he should at least be present to see it through the House of Commons.

speechtext: I have only one observation to make with regard to the statement of the minister. This legislation involves the payment of public money to this harbour board and contemplates the delivery of the securities of that board to the Minister of Finance. I submit that the Duncan report did not contemplate that sort of national port development; it contemplated a direct expenditure of public money for the purpose of developing the ports of St. John and Halifax.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Under a statutory commission. This contemplates a harbour commission, but the Duncan report contemplated and stated in terms a statutory commission. In my judgment Sir Andrew Rae Duncan had in mind a statutory commission which would be an administrative body, not a body charged with the responsibility of issuing securities which would not be of value to this country. If this harbour cannot earn 5 per cent upon $5,000,000, as it may not, and as is not intended it would by the Duncan report any more than Quebec has been able to do so, it seems to me an improper thing that it should issue securities and place them in the treasury against grants of public money, when we know that so far as the payment of interest is concerned the securities are of no real value. That is the point we endeavoured to make yesterday, and I cannot help but think that the principle with respect to both Halifax and St. John is not sound, because it imposes an obligation upon those ports
St. John Harbour Commission

which we do not expect they will be able to discharge. We have imposed such an obligation upon the port of Quebec, and obviously it is not expected that the port of Quebec will be able to discharge that obligation. So it does occur to me that if we are to make a national port, as the words were used by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan, we should do it directly, and not by this indirect means which is adopted for the purpose of placing in our treasury securities which are without value. That is the point I desire to make with the minister, because there is a very serious principle involved in it. That has led to all the difficulty in Quebec; there can be no doubt about that. If we had continued to expend public moneys at Quebec as we have done at other ports at the head of the lakes, without taking promises to pay from the port, the present situation would not have arisen. The difficulty with port administration under a commission is that they become political commissions rather than national port commissions; the minister knows that very much better than I, because in small communities such a commission is bound to be a political commission. We must remember that when the statute was first passed it contained a provision whereby at least one of the commissioners was elected by the community. I daresay the minister recalls those days when there was an election held for the selection of a commission by the ratepayers of the community. Now the real truth under existing conditions is that as soon as there is a change of government there is a change of the commission, and the harbour commission instead of being a body constituted to develop the port becomes nothing more or less than a political commission. I am not saying that of one government only; I am very careful not to do so, because virtue does not rest in one particular set of men and lack of it in another. The real fact is that the circumstances and conditions under which these commissions discharge their duties lend themselves to political purposes, very often to the finding of employment for political followers. That, as I say, is not applicable to one side more than to the other, but the fact remains thlat it operates against the efficiency of the commission. Take for instance the harbour of Montreal. A change of government in 1911 was followed by a change of the personnel of the commission, and there was a change of government in 1921, followed by another change of commission. There was a change of commissioners in the harbour of Quebec in the same way. The harbour of St. John, so far as the commission is concerned, is now dealt

with in the same way as Halifax. The commission is appointed from political followers pure and simple, all Liberals. Now a national port is not a Liberal port, it is not a Conservative port; it belongs to Liberals and Conservatives. Because a Liberal government is in power is no reason why only Liberals should find employment on the harbour commission.

speechtext:
Or even the whole of it.
If St. John harbour is developed as it should be in order, together with Halifax, to take care of transatlantic shipments, especially in the winter time, there is no reason to suppose that as regards the amount of money necessary to prepare the port of St. John for that transportation it cannot secure sufficient revenue to pay at least the interest, if not the sinking fund. St. John harbour is, or was prior to a year ago, the only harbour in Canada owned directly by a city. Under a royal charter that harbour was conceded to the city of St. John, and the Department of Marine and Fisheries had no control in any way over that harbour. Over a period of several years, considering that in years gone by, at least prior to 1910 or 1911, St. John harbour was not getting sufficient recognition from the different governments at Ottawa, the corporation of the city of St. John undertook to improve the harbour at its own expense, and to that end it expended in the neighbourhood of between $2,000,000 and $3,000,000. It paid the interest on that expenditure and it set aside a sinking fund to the extent that last year there was in that fund an amount of $667,000 to meet maturing bonds. Not only did it pay interest and provide sinking fund payments, but each year it had a surplus, and its surplus would have been greater had it not been that in 1925, St. John, seeing that it was necessary to divert Canadian export trade to Canadian ports and not being able to get a proper freight rate which would warrant grain going through that port, diminished its side wharfage and top wharfage charges on grain from six cents to one cent a bushel in order to encourage the western farmers to ship their freight through Canadian ports. Had St. John not done that, its surplus in 1925, 1926 and 1927, after meeting interest and sinking fund payments, would have been a great deal larger. But St. John was acting from a national point of view; its interest was the development of Canadian ports, and the encouragement of Canadian trade to go through Canadian ports. I think all will admit that it is diversity of freight that makes up the revenues of a port. Any port on the Atlantic that depends entirely for its revenue upon the shipment of grain cannot be a financial success. Last year 25,000,000 bushels of wheat passed through the port of St. John. It had six million tons of export trade and one and a half million tons of imports.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Is not the minister wrong about six million tons of exports other than grain?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I did not say other than
grain. Grain did not amount to more than 850,000 tons of the 6.000 000 tons exported. St. John's trade is not all transatlantic. St. John has a large exportation of farm products to other than transatlantic countries. Furthermore. for its size St. John is equipped to-day for the cattle trade in a way that no other port in Canada is equipped. There is room in our newly constructed sheds at St. John to-day to accommodate at one time 1.353 head of cattle. St. John has also some of the best frost-proof warehouses to take care of agricultural produce, such as potatoes and other produce which has to be shipped in winter to prevent perishing. With all these advantages, and with the amount of money that St. John is asking for to-day, $5,000,000 -it is true that they did ask for $10,000,000, which would have completed the program in five or six or perhaps seven years, and would have put the port in a position to handle double the grain and double the mixed freight which it is handling to-day-when you consider that Vancouver, with all its facilities and improvements, handled 43,000,000 bushels, I believe, of grain last year, and that St. John handled 25,000,000 bushels-and the quantity would have been much larger last fall and this winter had it not been for a restriction, if I may use that term, on the exportation of grain transatlantic-you begin to realize the possibilities of the harbour of St. John.
It is true that large sums of money have been expended by the government in the past on the harbour of St. John. I am not going to say that the money has always been judiciously expended. But leaving aside the Courtenay bay proposition and taking St. John harbour as we look upon it to-day, together with the improvements that are to be made on the west side, where the Canadian Pacific is bringing large quantities of grain and has not the facilities necessary to bring larger quantities, and considering that the Canadian National has no way of reaching the west side of the harbour except with the special privilege of running over the lines of the Caandian Pacific from east to west; considering also that St. John is prepared as a city to-day, if I can believe the officials of the city, the mayor and the commissioners, and I believe that I can, to expend still further sums of their own in aiding the railways and giving greater facilities in the way of a bridge across the harbour so that the

St. John Harbour Commission
Canadian National may have extended privileges on the west side-all these things considered, I feel that St. John deserves a great deal of praise for what it has done, and further that any sum of money which this parliament may vote to St. John will be judiciously expended.
The leader of the opposition referred to the political aspect of these commissions. It is true that when this new commission was appointed it was tainted with Liberalism.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Not tainted, surely.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
But it is also true that
the full harbour organization of the city of St. John, without regard to political affiliations, was taken over by the present harbour commission; not one single dismissal was made. Let me go further. The engineer in charge of the harbour works in St. John to-day is the same engineer who was in charge of expenditures in the main harbour, the present harbour for which we are seeking improvements. He is the engineer of the Department of Public Works who has been in charge of those works during the last eight or ten years. His name is Mr. Gray, and I think I am safe in stating that no more efficient and no more capable engineer on harbour construction and improvements can be found in the Dominion of Canada. He has had a vast experience. No engineer could possibly be obtained to-day who knows more about the peculiar tidal conditions in the harbour of St. John and the bay of Fundy than does the present engineer, due to the long experience he has had there.
The work in St. John perhaps will be more costly than in any other harbour in the Dominion, for this reason: the heavy rise and fall of the Fundy tides necessitates the construction of piers of a much greater depth and far more costly than are required in any other harbour in the Dominion.
When the bill is in committee I expect to go into further details, but lest I may not have that opportunity let me say now that so congested are conditions in the harbour of St. John that in December, 1926, and January, 1927, ships coming in for grain and other cargoes lost no less than 155 days demurrage, mostly because they were lying in the stream awaiting berths. That is the condition. St. John and Halifax are the only two ports on the Atlantic coast through which Canadian trade can go in and out during the winter season. May I point this out also, that in the winter time the United States ports of Portland and Boston are losing so much of their trade to Halifax and
fMr. Veniot.]
St. John that there is a movement on foot in the senate at Washington to devise some means of preventing this loss. To my mind Halifax and St. John, being the only Atlantic ports that are open the year round, like Vancouver on the Pacific, are really our two national ports on the Atlantic coast, and for that if no other reason they should receive all the encouragement that I feel this house will give them.
I wish to thank hon. members on both sides for the very generous support they accorded to the maritime provinces last winter when their case was before the house. I do not accept the remarks of the hon. leader of the opposition as made in a spirit of criticism or opposition to this grant, but rather in an endeavour to find a better method of carrying on these works. Speaking for myself, I court the most rigorous investigation of all expenditures for the development of the harbours of the maritime provinces.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would
not have the committee think from what the hon. leader of the opposition has suggested with regard to the personnel of the commission that I do not consider those gentlemen in every way qualified for their job.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I did not mention their qualifications-except politically.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Is it a qualification?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
My hon. friend stated that they were politicians, leaving the impression on the committee that they were appointed primarily because they were adherents of the Liberal party. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin) does not happen to know those gentlemen personally as I do. The leader of the opposition probably knows them pretty well, andi I think he will join with me in what I am about to say, because I quite realize that he did not single them out particularly because of their political views. But I want to take the committee into my confidence to convince them that political considerations had not primarily to do with the appointments. In the city of Halifax there has been a good deal of criticism of the government for their selection of those gentlemen, simply because they were not regarded as dyed-in-the-wool, hard-shell partisans. It seems you are damned if you do and damned if you don't. Our endeavour was to select as commissioners those who had the widest experience and the best qualifications, which, combined with their personality and long residence in the city, admirably adapted them to discharge the duties of their office. Mr. Peter R. Jack, the

St. John Harbour Commission
chairman of the commission, was bom in the city of Halifax; he is a bright, energetic, young business man and has been associated with many of the most progressive activities of the city, and I think everyone agrees that he is well qualified for the position. Mr C. W. Ackhurst is a shipping man, has been connected with the waterfront all his life, and is a very able and efficient man of business. Mr. John Murphy was controller for two or three terms, and then mayor of the city for two terms, and is regarded as one of the ablest of its citizens, thoroughly imbued with its civic spirit and point of view. Those are the type of men appointed to administer the harbour. Tree, they happen to be Liberals, but I do not think that should be regarded as a disqualification, provided they have the proper business experience and capacity to discharge the duties of their office. That a man happens to be an adherent of the party in power has never been regarded as a disqualification for office by this or any other government, provided he possessed the requisite qualifications for appointment.
I may be permitted to read to the committee the resolution which was passed by the Halifax board of trade immediately after those gentlemen were appointed. And I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that the Halifax board of trade is not by any means composed wholly of supporters of the Liberal party.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Judging by the last
election.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Judging by the last election, as my hon. friend interjects. I do not think there can be the least doubt about that. At any rate I have no doubt myself. This is the resolution:
This board appreciates Hon. J. L. Ralston telegraphing them of the appointment and personnel of the Halifax harbour commission and wishes to commend him on his selection and assure him of the board's assistance and cooperation; also.
The board wishes to congratulate the harbour commissioners on their appointment and assure them of the fullest co-operation and assistance.
That is the personnel of the Halifax harbour commission to whom this house will be asked to vote a certain sum of money when the bill is introduced, and I can honestly, sincerely, and frankly say that I believe those men are amply qualified to discharge the duties of their office, even though they may happen to be adherents of the Liberal party.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to have to make another observation in respect to this matter. The point I was endeavouring to make was that the political *character of the commission involves political
patronage in the expenditure of moneys, and all we on this side have been suggesting is the desirability of assuring one hundred per cent of effort for every dollar of expenditure.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend? If the statutory commission is appointed at all, would my hon. friend suggest that something should be inserted in the act that the appointees be not supporters of the government?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
No. The Minister of
National Defence is too astute to put that construction on what was said. I pointed out that originally the constitution of harbour commissions provided for the election of at least one member. That was done away with and the appointment of partisans substituted. I was careful to say that either party would do the same thing; I did not say that my hon. friend's party was responsible.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: I did not suggest it.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
I pointed out that the appointment of your own partisans assured patronage being relied upon in connection with expenditures, and we in this house know that in small communities the tendency is to prevent a hundred cents of effort resulting from a dollar's expenditure. This being a national port, so vastly different from anything else we have, a port in which we are all interested, I am sure the minister realizes that the pressure put upon him-the minister from Nova Scotia-to have his friends looked after with respect to the work of the harbour will be very great indeed. I am sorry to say it is so, human nature being as it is. I see my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) smiles, for he knows just what it means in New Brunswick-and just what it will mean in Nova Scotia also. That patronage evil might be overcome in two ways. First, t'he personnel of the commission should not wholly reflect the view of the party in power. This practice is followed in England, as my hon. friend knows. For example, the head of the port authority of London on one occasion was certainly everything else than a supporter of the particular government of the day, and the government itself, except through the Board of Trade, had nothing to do with the matter at all. Secondly, it is desirable that this parliament should have some control over that expenditure, direct through the Auditor General and through the public accounts committee. My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and I placed that before the house two years ago with some degree of force. Once more I say to the Postmaster General



St. John Harbour Commission
so far as Now Brunswick is concerned, that every hon. member in this house is to my knowledge in favour of these expenditures in St. John; but what we fear is that the result of this effort will not be to get 100 cents of value for 100 cents of expenditure. And I need hardly say to my hon. friend that those of us who are familiar with what has transpired in days gone by in the public accounts committee and in other investigations as well have some reason to realize that public moneys expended, not by the city of St. John but by the government of Canada, in connection with dredging contracts for instance, were not wholly beyond suspicion. I will use only the words that came out in connection with one or two investigations, and the Postmaster General will understand the rest of it. And that was not limited to any particular class of individuals.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext: Or to any particular party.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Exactly. I want the
minister to understand that I was only suggesting that St. John might not pay interest. But if we expect to recover the interest it will involve the payment of tolls, wharfages and other charges such as might make it disadvantageous to the port; and I want the lowest possible tolls to be exacted and the lowest possible dues to be charged, for a reason I did not care to mention, but which I communicated to my hon. friend to my right, namely, the effort of seaboard ports on the United States front to take away from us a part of the traffic we now have. For this reason we shall have to maintain the lowest possible tolls and charges to insure success in our operations. Therefore we must not regard these moneys as loans in connection with which interest and sinking fund are to be taken care of, but rather as contributions made by the parliament of Canada towards the development of a national port. I am sorry if I did not make that clear, for it was the purpose of my observation. Regardless of what the return may be, the most efficient method should be pursued, under the direction of the most competent engineers, and the charges imposed should have some regard to the service rendered, irrespective of the question of interest or sinking fund. I do not think the minister should place in the treasury of the country the bonds and debentures of these commissions and find himself, in a year or two, faced with the statement, "We are unable to pay interest because the tolls are not sufficient to enable us to do so." I do not want to see this port labouring under the handicap that has hampered the port of

Quebec, as indicated by the minister yesterday. That is the position I take with respect to this matter and which I wish to make quite clear. The Postmaster General misunderstood me if he thought for a moment that I suggested that the harbour of St. John could not earn charges, for it undoubtedly could if the tolls were high enough. But that might have an adverse effect on its traffic, and our business is to provide traffic, making these facilities thoroughly effective and useful in the national interest of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Was it not argued yesterday
that the port of Quebec should earn enough to pay interest on the money?

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
What was argued was
that the port of Quebec, had it been efficiently conducted and a proper ratio of gross and net earnings preserved, as has been done in the case of St. John, would have paid interest on the present investment. St. John last year not only took care of interest and sinking fund but it had a surplus of $40,000. That port had net earnings of $218,000, including interest and sinking fund charges, as against $257,000 odd of gross earnings. The argument that has not been answered and cannot be answered is that the expenditures in Quebec were out of all proportion, as between net and gross earnings, to any other port in Canada. And what is more, there is the report of the audit board, set down in black and white, to which no answer was made. That report bears out the argument.

maintopic: ST. JOHN HARBOUR COMMISSION LOAN OF $5,000,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Regarding the resolution before the committee with reference to the proposed loan to the harbour commission of the port of St. John, I wish to place myself on record as strongly supporting the proposal. The harbour of St. John was taken over by the present board on August 1 last. The board as at present constituted is composed of men of ability and character, together with an engineer of the highest standing in the profession-I refer to Mr. Alexander Gray, late Dominion engineer at the port of St. John. The loan asked for is not as large as was recommended by the harbour board, having been reduced by half; and it is to cover a period of three years. The vote as at present proposed is the outcome of the creation of the Duncan commission, whose report bearing on the question of port development and equipment contains the following statement at page 29:
We are satisfied that neither at Halifax nor at St. John-although developments at St. John have been more extensive than at Halifax'-is

Halifax Harbour Commission
it possible, in present circumstances, to secure adequate port development. We recommend that, in respect of each of these two harbours, the federal government should establish a statutory harbour commission, whose business it would be to see that the port facilities are developed on such a scale as will gradually-but by no means slowly-create channels through which trade can expand both winter and summer. The development of a port is as much a matter of mechanical and technical equipment, business organization and practical administration. as is the development of any extensive manufacturing or industrial business.
The winter port traffic started in St. John in 1901. In that year the total revenue of the port was $40,630. In 1927 the total levenue was $257,704.97. During the last ten years the development of the winter port traffic has been hampered by lack of adequate berthing facilities. In 1926-27 one ship had to wait twelve days for a berth and another eight days. Due to lack of facilities in the winter port season of 1926-27 transatlantic steamers were held up for a total of 155 days. With the present inadequate equipment much business is lost. Berths, warehouse room and elevator storage are urgently needed if the business of the port is to increase at a normal rate. The proposed improvements call for pier accommodation, representing from five to six steamships. A grain elevator is urgently needed as are also transit sheds with office accommodation. The estimated cost is $5,000,000, the work to extend over a period of three years. I am convinced that a straight government loan would be much better than an obligation on the part of the harbour board. I should not like to have the board undertake any obligation on which they could not meet interest.
I might say in support of what the Postmaster General has stated that undoubtedly, with the new facilities that will be provided, and having in mind the additional expenditure which later on will probably be involved, through the erection of a bridge across the river, the Canadian National and the new terminals which will also be established will greatly facilitate the export and import business. I trust that the house will give the most favouralbe consideration to this resolution and provide the St. John with what is necessary to assist it in its worty effort to develop trade through that port.
Resolution reported, read the second time and! concurred in. Mr. Cardin thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 216, to provide for a loan to the St. John Harbour Commissioners.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: LOAN OF $500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
As this makes a total of
over $14,000,000 which is to be spent for the development of these eastern ports, I would ask the government if they have any policy with regard to the movement of grain from the west, since these developments are made particularly to handle that business? If the lower rates on the Transcontinental railway have any effect at all they will undoubtedly benefit the ports on the Atlantic coast, and in that case it seems very unwise to spend such a large sum of money on the port of Quebec since the facilities of that port never have been used to their full extent. Do the government intend that the port of Quebec or the ports on the Atlantic shall receive a greater amount of grain, or what do they intend?
I would also point out that we have seen fit to direct a great part of our wheat through United States ports as the most feasible route to the markets of the world. If there is to be winter handling, which the Minister of Railways said yesterday was so profitable, why should we store wheat at Quebec? If the grain is to move over the Transcontinental railway at all it is certain to go to Halifax or St. John, and it seems to me that the government should formulate some direct policy with regard to those ports rather than spend such sums as $5,000,000 and $8,500,000 indiscriminately on the same port without knowing whether or not it will be used to its capacity.

subtopic: LOAN OF $500,000 FOR TERMINAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
Perhaps I might be permitted to answer my hon, friend in that regard without attempting to lay down any fixed. policy on behalf of the government, because these are largely matters of development. I would point out that there is a difference between making provision for winter storage and for winter handling. In the nature of things there will be comparatively little winter storage at a port which is open during the winter; there is comparatively little winter storage at Vancouver or at Halifax and St.
(Mr. Cardin.]
John. On the other hand, at interior ports, both in the United States and in Canada, there is an increasing tendency to provide for winter storage in order that grain may be in a strategic location for spring shipment. In that connection it has been found more advantageous than would be the case, in the national interest of Canada, to store grain for the winter in United States winter storage terminals. A number of years ago a company, with which I believe the leader of the opposition was connected, was a pioneer in the direction of providing winter storage for grain within Canada, instead of using to such a large extent United States facilities located at United States lake ports, and other interior ports, for that purpose. And so in Canada we have been gradually building up two types of facilities, one for the continuous handling of grain at ports which are open the year round, and the other winter storage facilities as close as possible to the channels of world trade at places which are not open the year round but are closed for a considerable portion of it. Montreal has gone in for winter storage to a far greater extent in recent years than formerly. Utilization of the winter storage at Quebec, filled to almost its full capacity for the first time, is further evidence of the use which the trade and the pools will make of winter storage as near as possible to the outlet of navigation. If the trade is there for them I think it is of considerable advantage to have in Canada enough winter storage to take care of Canadian grain, and as a matter of fact as much American grain as can come. That is the broad answer I make to my hon. friend.

That the Minister of Finance may provide for the purposes of the commission by the sale or other disposition of securities of the commission, guaranteed as hereinafter provided, an amount or amounts not to exceed in the aggregate $3,000,000, or he may, with the approval of the governor in council, pay to the commission, out of the consolidated revenue fund, such sum or sums, not exceeding $3,000,000. as may be required for said purposes, or may make such provision partly in one way and partly in the other. The governor in council may authorize the guarantee of the payment of principal of and interest on any such securities, the proceeds to be deposited to the credit of the Minister of Finance in trust for the commission and released by the minister in his discretion for the purposes of the act;
3.	That the Minister of Finance may provide out of the consolidated revenue fund such sums as may be required to pay interest on the said securities and also such sums as are required for the purpose of establishing a sinking fund or for retiring the said securities by annual instalments:
4.	That the provisions of the Expropriation Act. instead of the Railway Act shall be made applicable to expropriation proceedings of the commission.

subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext: Would the Prime Minister make a short explanation of the proposal?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: IMPROVEMENT AND BEAUTIFICATION OF OTTAWA
speechtext:
The bill to be based on the resolution proposes to reduce from $250,000 to $200,000 the amount granted to the commission as an annual appropriation. It is estimated that at the present time something like $150,000 a year is required for the maintenance of the work already done by the commission on parks and driveways. For the period of time to which reference is made in the resolution it is probable that an amount equal at least to $200,000 a year will be required for maintenance alone. It is proposed that any small amount over and above what is required for maintenance should go to meet small incidental capital expenditures in connection with the work of the commission,

Federal District Commission
such for example as the construction of greenhouses. The rest of the resolution is a proposal that there should be voted by parliament for capital expenditures by the commission, a total sum of 13,000,000, to be provided either by payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, or by the' issue of securities to be redeemed over a period of thirty years. The intention of the government, if parliament approves, is to provide at once, by way of capital expenditure, chargeable to the public debt, the sums necessary to meet the cost of expropriating what is now known as the Russell house property, including the Russell theatre property. Other capital expenditures would be met by the issue of securities to be redeemed over the period of thirty years. It is hoped that parliament will approve a plan of providing for the construction of a confederation park in the centre of the city by the expropriation of a few buildings at present situated between Sparks street, Laurier avenue, Elgin street and the canal. It is not proposed that all of the buildings will be expropriated but only some that can be taken over to the advantage of all concerned. At the present time, as hon. members know, there is on Laurier avenue a large open space in the nature of a park, known as Cartier square. Below Cartier square there is the property, owned by the Ontario government, on which the Normal model school and Normal school buildings are situated. Adjoining parliament hill is Major Hill park. The members of the commission feel that if the property between Cartier square and Major Hill park could be acquired and transformed into a park there would be in the heart of the capital, one large central park, and this open space would lend a character to the whole city which would have its effect in the ultimate beautification and development of the capital.
